We're working as partners, not as client and contractor. One rule before the task:

Not knowing something is not a failure. Saying "I couldn't verify this" or
"I don't have a real source for that" is a completely acceptable, useful answer
- it's information, not a dead end. The ONLY real failure is inventing something
(a source, a number, a quote, a repo, a bug) to make the answer sound more complete or
more impressive than it honestly is. You don't need to satisfy me with a
confident-sounding answer. You need to be honest with me about what you actually
know.

If you find something, cite it and quote what it actually says - don't
paraphrase a source into numbers it may not contain. If you don't find
something concrete, say so plainly and reason from what you do have instead.
An explicit "uncertain" section at the end is welcome and doesn't count against
the answer.

Find real, documented post-mortems of major cloud outages in 2025 (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Cloudflare). For each, cite the provider's own incident report and quote what it says the root cause was.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Here are the real, documented post-mortems I was able to find from the provided search results for major cloud outages in 2025. The search results contained detailed incident reports from Azure and Cloudflare, but did not contain any AWS or Google Cloud outages.

### Azure Front Door (October 29, 2025)
Azure experienced a global outage affecting its Front Door and CDN services, which took down portals and Microsoft 365 services for approximately 8.5 hours. The provider traced the root cause back to a latent bug triggered by normal customer configuration changes.

SOURCE: https://postmortem.io/incidents/azure--2025-10-29--azure-front-door-global-connectivity-dns-issues/ | QUOTE: "A specific sequence of customer configuration changes, performed across two different control plane build versions, resulted in incompatible customer configuration metadata being generated." | CLAIM: The root cause of the Azure Front Door outage was incompatible configuration metadata generated by valid customer configuration changes across different control plane builds.

### Cloudflare Outage (November 18, 2025)
Cloudflare experienced a global network outage that prevented users from accessing customer sites. The root cause was tied to a database permission change that inadvertently broke a file size limit in their Bot Management system.

SOURCE: https://postmortem.io/incidents/cloudflare--2025-11-18--global-network-outage-bot-management/ | QUOTE: "Instead, it was triggered by a change to one of our database systems’ permissions which caused the database to output multiple entries into a “feature file” used by our Bot Management system." | CLAIM: The root cause of the Cloudflare November 18 outage was a database permission change that caused duplicate entries in a Bot Management feature file.

SOURCE: https://blog.cloudflare.com/5-december-2025-outage/ | QUOTE: "The issue was not caused, directly or indirectly, by a cyber attack on Cloudflare’s systems or malicious activity of any kind. Instead, it was triggered by changes being made to our body parsing logic while attempting to detect and mitigate an industry-wide vulnerability disclosed this week in React Server Components." | CLAIM: The root cause of the Cloudflare December 5 outage was an error state triggered by changes to body parsing logic intended to mitigate a React Server Components vulnerability.

SOURCE: https://blog.cloudflare.com/deep-dive-into-cloudflares-sept-12-dashboard-and-api-outage/ | QUOTE: "The incident’s impact stemmed from several issues, but the immediate trigger was a bug in the dashboard. This bug caused repeated, unnecessary calls to the Tenant Service API." | CLAIM: The root cause of the Cloudflare September 12 dashboard and API outage was a frontend bug causing repeated, unnecessary API calls that overwhelmed the Tenant Service.

SOURCE: https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-1-1-1-1-incident-on-july-14-2025/ | QUOTE: "On June 6, during a release to prepare a service topology for a future DLS service, a configuration error was introduced: the prefixes associated with the 1.1.1.1 Resolver service were inadvertently included alongside the prefixes that were intended for the new DLS service." | CLAIM: The root cause of the Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 Resolver outage on July 14 was a dormant configuration error from June 6 that misrouted IP prefixes.

### Uncertain / Not Found
The search results provided to me did not contain any incident reports or post-mortems for AWS or Google Cloud outages in 2025. I cannot verify whether major documented outages occurred for those specific providers in 2025 based on the information I have access to here.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: AWS outage post-mortems or incident reports in 2025.
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: Google Cloud outage post-mortems or incident reports in 2025.

*(Note: The Azure Front Door incident report was sourced via [postmortem.io](https://postmortem.io/incidents/azure--2025-10-29--azure-front-door-global-connectivity-dns-issues/), which republished Microsoft Azure's Post Incident Review. The Cloudflare incident reports were sourced via [postmortem.io](https://postmortem.io/incidents/cloudflare--2025-11-18--global-network-outage-bot-management/) and [blog.cloudflare.com](https://blog.cloudflare.com/5-december-2025-outage/).)*
